notes:
1. Basic Facts
  • Forest resources include trees, shrubs, herbs, wildlife habitats and ecological services obtained from forest ecosystems.
  • Forests provide both direct products and indirect environmental benefits.
  • They are renewable resources only when extraction does not exceed regeneration.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Forest → Renewable Only Under Sustainable Use

2. Importance of Forests

Forests provide:

  • Timber.
  • Fuelwood.
  • Fodder.
  • Bamboo.
  • Medicinal plants.
  • Gums and resins.
  • Fruits and fibres.
  • Wildlife habitat.
  • Soil protection.
  • Water conservation.
  • Carbon storage.
3. Ecological Functions of Forests

Forests help:

  • Reduce soil erosion.
  • Regulate runoff.
  • Improve infiltration.
  • Protect watersheds.
  • Moderate local climate.
  • Maintain biodiversity.
  • Store carbon.
  • Support nutrient cycling.
4. Forest and Soil Conservation
  • Tree roots bind soil particles.
  • Vegetation reduces the direct impact of rainfall.
  • Forest litter slows surface runoff.
  • Forest cover therefore helps reduce soil erosion.
5. Forests and Water Cycle

Forests influence:

  • Interception of rainfall.
  • Infiltration.
  • Evapotranspiration.
  • Groundwater recharge.
  • Stream flow.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Forest Cover → Watershed Protection

6. Forests and Climate
  • Forests absorb carbon dioxide through photosynthesis.
  • Carbon is stored in:
  • Trees.
  • Roots.
  • Litter.
  • Soil.
  • Forest loss can release stored carbon.
7. Carbon Sink
  • A carbon sink absorbs more carbon than it releases.
  • Growing forests can act as carbon sinks.
📌 Must-Memorise

Forest → Important Terrestrial Carbon Sink

8. Forest Ecosystem

A forest ecosystem contains:

  • Producers.
  • Consumers.
  • Decomposers.
  • Soil.
  • Water.
  • Climatic components.
9. Natural Vegetation
  • Natural vegetation refers to plant communities that develop mainly under natural environmental conditions.
  • Climate, soil and relief strongly influence its distribution.
10. Major Controls of Forest Distribution

Important controls include:

  • Rainfall.
  • Temperature.
  • Altitude.
  • Soil.
  • Relief.
  • Length of dry season.
  • Human disturbance.
11. Rainfall and Forest Type

Broad relationship:

  • Very high rainfall → Evergreen forests.
  • Moderate rainfall → Moist deciduous forests.
  • Lower rainfall → Dry deciduous forests.
  • Very low rainfall → Thorn and scrub vegetation.
12. Temperature and Vegetation
  • Tropical forests occur in warm lowlands.
  • Temperate forests occur at cooler elevations.
  • Alpine vegetation occurs above the tree line.
13. Altitudinal Zonation
  • Mountain vegetation changes with altitude.
  • Rising altitude produces climatic changes similar in some respects to moving from tropical to colder latitudes.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Altitude ↑ → Vegetation Type Changes

14. Major Natural Vegetation Types of India

Important types include:

  • Tropical evergreen forests.
  • Tropical semi-evergreen forests.
  • Tropical moist deciduous forests.
  • Tropical dry deciduous forests.
  • Tropical thorn forests.
  • Montane forests.
  • Littoral and swamp forests.
  • Mangrove forests.
15. Tropical Evergreen Forests
  • Tropical evergreen forests occur in areas of high rainfall and high temperature.
  • They remain green throughout the year.
  • Trees do not shed all their leaves at the same time.
📌 Must-Memorise

Evergreen Forest → No Distinct Leafless Season

16. Conditions for Tropical Evergreen Forest

They generally require:

  • High annual rainfall.
  • High humidity.
  • Warm temperature.
  • Short or absent dry season.
17. Distribution of Evergreen Forests

Important regions include:

  • Western Ghats.
  • Northeastern India.
  • Andaman and Nicobar Islands.
18. Structure of Evergreen Forest
  • Vegetation is dense.
  • Trees may form several vertical layers.
  • Sunlight penetration to the ground can be limited.
  • Climbers and epiphytes are common.
19. Evergreen Tree Species

Important species include:

  • Ebony.
  • Rosewood.
  • Mahogany.
  • Aini.
  • Hopea.
  • Mesua and other regional species.
20. Rosewood
  • Rosewood is an important valuable hardwood.
  • It occurs in high-rainfall forest regions, including parts of the Western Ghats.
21. Ebony
  • Ebony is a dense, dark hardwood.
  • It is associated with tropical evergreen forests.
22. Tropical Semi-Evergreen Forests
  • Semi-evergreen forests occur in transitional zones between evergreen and moist deciduous forests.
  • They contain a mixture of evergreen and deciduous species.
23. Semi-Evergreen Distribution

They occur in parts of:

  • Western Ghats.
  • Northeastern India.
  • Andaman and Nicobar Islands.
24. Tropical Deciduous Forests
  • Tropical deciduous forests are India's most widespread natural forest type.
  • Trees shed leaves during a distinct dry season to conserve water.
📌 Must-Memorise

Most Widespread Indian Forest Type → Tropical Deciduous

25. Monsoon Forest
  • Tropical deciduous forests are also called monsoon forests.
  • Their growth is strongly influenced by seasonal rainfall.
26. Two Major Deciduous Types

They are broadly divided into:

  • Moist deciduous forests.
  • Dry deciduous forests.
27. Moist Deciduous Forests
  • Moist deciduous forests occur in areas receiving moderate to high rainfall.
  • They are less dense than evergreen forests.
  • Many trees shed leaves during the dry season.
28. Distribution of Moist Deciduous Forest

Important regions include:

  • Eastern slopes of Western Ghats.
  • Odisha.
  • Jharkhand.
  • Chhattisgarh.
  • Eastern Madhya Pradesh.
  • Himalayan foothills.
  • Parts of northeastern India.
29. Important Moist Deciduous Species

Important species include:

  • Teak.
  • Sal.
  • Shisham.
  • Bamboo.
  • Sandalwood in suitable southern regions.
  • Mahua.
30. Teak
  • Teak is one of India's most valuable timber trees.
  • It is strongly associated with deciduous forests.
  • It is widely used for:
  • Furniture.
  • Construction.
  • Shipbuilding.
📌 Must-Memorise

Teak → Deciduous Forest → Valuable Timber

31. Teak Distribution

Important teak regions include parts of:

  • Madhya Pradesh.
  • Maharashtra.
  • Karnataka.
  • Tamil Nadu.
  • Kerala.
  • Chhattisgarh.
32. Sal
  • Sal is another major Indian hardwood tree.
  • It is especially important in northern and eastern deciduous forests.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Sal → Northern/Eastern Deciduous Forest

33. Sal Distribution

Sal is common in parts of:

  • Jharkhand.
  • Chhattisgarh.
  • Odisha.
  • West Bengal.
  • Uttarakhand foothills.
  • Uttar Pradesh.
  • Madhya Pradesh.
34. Teak vs Sal

Teak:

  • Strongly associated with central and peninsular India.

Sal:

  • More characteristic of northern, eastern and central moist deciduous belts.
35. Dry Deciduous Forests
  • Dry deciduous forests occur where rainfall is lower and the dry season is longer.
  • Tree cover is more open.
  • Grasses and shrubs are common.
36. Distribution of Dry Deciduous Forests

They occur in parts of:

  • Interior Peninsular India.
  • Madhya Pradesh.
  • Maharashtra.
  • Karnataka.
  • Telangana.
  • Andhra Pradesh.
  • Tamil Nadu.
  • Rajasthan's wetter margins.
  • Uttar Pradesh and Bihar dry zones.
37. Dry Deciduous Species

Important species include:

  • Teak.
  • Palas.
  • Tendu.
  • Khair.
  • Acacia.
  • Neem in disturbed landscapes.
38. Tendu
  • Tendu leaves are widely used in the traditional bidi industry.
  • Tendu is an important non-timber forest product.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Tendu Leaves → Bidi

39. Mahua
  • Mahua is an important tree of central Indian forests.
  • Its flowers and seeds have food, oil and livelihood uses.
  • It is culturally and economically important to many forest communities.
40. Bamboo
  • Bamboo is botanically a grass.
  • It is one of India's most important forest resources.
  • It is used for:
  • Construction.
  • Paper and pulp.
  • Furniture.
  • Handicrafts.
  • Scaffolding.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Bamboo → Grass, Not Tree Botanically

41. Tropical Thorn Forests
  • Thorn forests develop under low rainfall and high evaporation.
  • Vegetation is sparse.
  • Plants are adapted to conserve water.
42. Distribution of Thorn Forests

Important regions include:

  • Rajasthan.
  • Gujarat.
  • Southwestern Punjab.
  • Haryana.
  • Rain-shadow areas of Peninsular India.
  • Dry parts of Tamil Nadu.
43. Thorn Forest Adaptations

Plants commonly have:

  • Small leaves.
  • Thorns.
  • Thick bark.
  • Deep roots.
  • Succulent stems in some species.
44. Thorn Forest Species

Important examples include:

  • Acacia.
  • Babool.
  • Khejri.
  • Ber.
  • Cactus-like xerophytic plants.
  • Euphorbia.
45. Khejri
  • Khejri is an important tree of Rajasthan's dry regions.
  • It is well adapted to arid conditions.
  • It has major ecological and cultural importance.
46. Xerophytes
  • Xerophytes are plants adapted to dry conditions.
  • They reduce water loss and survive prolonged drought.
📌 Must-Memorise

Xerophyte → Dry-Climate Plant

47. Montane Forests
  • Montane forests occur in mountainous regions.
  • Vegetation changes with altitude, temperature and rainfall.
48. Himalayan Vegetation Zonation

Broad altitudinal sequence includes:

  • Subtropical forests at lower elevations.
  • Temperate broadleaf and conifer forests higher up.
  • Subalpine forests.
  • Alpine vegetation above the tree line.
49. Subtropical Himalayan Forests

Important vegetation includes:

  • Chir pine.
  • Broadleaf forests in wetter zones.
  • Subtropical scrub in drier areas.
50. Chir Pine
  • Chir pine is common in parts of the lower and middle Himalayas.
  • It occurs in relatively dry subtropical mountain zones.
51. Temperate Forests

Temperate Himalayan species include:

  • Oak.
  • Deodar.
  • Fir.
  • Spruce.
  • Cedar.
  • Maple in suitable zones.
52. Deodar
  • Deodar is a valuable Himalayan conifer.
  • It is common in the western Himalayas.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Deodar → Western Himalayas

53. Oak
  • Oak forests occur in moist temperate Himalayan zones.
  • Oak supports soil moisture and watershed protection.
54. Fir and Spruce
  • Fir and spruce are coniferous trees of cooler Himalayan elevations.
  • They are important components of temperate and subalpine forests.
55. Alpine Vegetation
  • Above the tree line, forests give way to:
  • Alpine shrubs.
  • Grasses.
  • Meadows.
  • At still higher elevations, permanent snow and bare rock dominate.
56. Alpine Meadows
  • Alpine meadows are high-altitude grasslands.
  • They provide seasonal grazing areas in Himalayan regions.
57. Shola Forests
  • Shola forests are patches of montane evergreen forest found in high valleys of the southern Western Ghats.
  • They occur together with montane grasslands.
📌 Tamil Nadu Must-Memorise

Shola Forest → Southern Western Ghats

58. Shola-Grassland Ecosystem

Important locations include highlands of:

  • Nilgiris.
  • Anaimalai.
  • Palani Hills.
  • Other southern Western Ghats.
59. Shola Importance

Sholas help:

  • Store water.
  • Feed streams.
  • Protect high-altitude biodiversity.
  • Reduce soil erosion.
60. Littoral Forests
  • Littoral vegetation occurs near coasts.
  • It is adapted to sandy, saline and wind-exposed conditions.
61. Swamp Forests
  • Swamp forests occur in waterlogged areas.
  • They include freshwater and tidal swamp vegetation.
62. Mangrove Forests
  • Mangroves are salt-tolerant forests found along tropical and subtropical coasts.
  • They grow in:
  • Estuaries.
  • Deltas.
  • Tidal creeks.
  • Mudflats.
📌 Must-Memorise

Mangrove → Tidal Saline Coastal Forest

63. Mangrove Adaptations

Mangroves possess adaptations such as:

  • Salt tolerance.
  • Special aerial roots.
  • Prop roots.
  • Pneumatophores.
  • Vivipary in many species.
64. Pneumatophores
  • Pneumatophores are specialised aerial roots that project above waterlogged soil.
  • They help roots obtain oxygen.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Pneumatophore → Mangrove Breathing Root

65. Prop Roots
  • Prop roots extend from stems or branches into the soil.
  • They provide support in soft tidal mud.
66. Vivipary
  • Vivipary means seeds begin germinating while still attached to the parent plant.
  • It is an adaptation seen in several mangroves.
67. Sundarbans
  • Sundarbans is the largest and best-known mangrove region associated with the Ganga-Brahmaputra-Meghna delta.
  • It extends across India and Bangladesh.
  • The Indian portion lies in West Bengal.
📌 Must-Memorise

Sundarbans → Mangrove → West Bengal/Bangladesh

68. Sundari Tree
  • The Sundarbans are traditionally associated with the Sundari tree.
  • The region derives its name partly from this vegetation association.
69. Other Important Mangrove Regions

Mangroves occur in:

  • Mahanadi delta.
  • Godavari delta.
  • Krishna delta.
  • Andaman and Nicobar Islands.
  • Gulf of Kachchh.
  • Tamil Nadu coast.
70. Tamil Nadu Mangroves

Important mangrove areas include:

  • Pichavaram.
  • Muthupet.
  • Gulf of Mannar/Palk Bay-associated coastal wetlands in selected areas.
📌 Tamil Nadu Must-Memorise

Pichavaram + Muthupet → Tamil Nadu Mangroves

71. Pichavaram Mangroves
  • Pichavaram lies near the Chidambaram-Cuddalore region.
  • It is associated with the Vellar-Coleroon estuarine system.
  • It contains a complex network of tidal channels.
🔗 Tamil Nadu Key Link

Pichavaram → Vellar-Coleroon Region

72. Muthupet Mangroves
  • Muthupet lies along the southeastern Tamil Nadu coast.
  • It is associated with the Kaveri delta coastal region.
  • It forms an important mangrove and lagoon ecosystem.
🔗 Tamil Nadu Key Link

Muthupet → Kaveri Delta Coast

73. Mangrove Ecological Importance

Mangroves:

  • Protect coasts from erosion.
  • Reduce wave energy.
  • Buffer storm surges.
  • Provide fish nursery grounds.
  • Store large amounts of carbon.
  • Support birds and marine organisms.
74. Blue Carbon
  • Blue carbon is carbon stored in coastal and marine ecosystems such as:
  • Mangroves.
  • Seagrass beds.
  • Salt marshes.
📌 TNPSC Advanced Fact

Mangroves → Blue Carbon Ecosystem

75. Forest Classification by Legal Status

Forests in India have traditionally been legally classified into categories such as:

  • Reserved forests.
  • Protected forests.
  • Unclassed forests.
76. Reserved Forests
  • Reserved forests receive the highest degree of legal protection among these traditional categories.
  • Activities are restricted unless specifically permitted.
📌 Must-Memorise

Reserved Forest → Highest Protection in Traditional Classification

77. Protected Forests
  • Protected forests are legally protected, but permitted rights and uses may differ from reserved forests.
78. Unclassed Forests
  • Unclassed forests are forests or wastelands not included in reserved or protected categories.
  • Their ownership may vary.
79. Forest Cover vs Recorded Forest Area
  • Recorded forest area is land legally recorded as forest.
  • Forest cover refers to land actually covered by tree canopy according to a specified assessment method.
  • The two are not identical.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Recorded Forest Area ≠ Forest Cover

80. Tree Cover
  • Tree cover generally refers to tree patches outside areas classified as forest cover under the relevant mapping definition.
  • Examples can include:
  • Farm trees.
  • Roadside trees.
  • Orchards in some contexts.
  • Urban trees.
81. Forest Density

Forest canopy density is often broadly described as:

  • Very dense.
  • Moderately dense.
  • Open forest.

Exact statistical definitions should be read from the latest official assessment when numbers are asked.

82. Social Forestry
  • Social forestry refers to growing trees outside conventional forests to meet local needs and reduce pressure on natural forests.
📌 Must-Memorise

Social Forestry → Trees for Community Needs

83. Objectives of Social Forestry

It aims to provide:

  • Fuelwood.
  • Fodder.
  • Small timber.
  • Environmental protection.
  • Rural employment.
84. Major Components of Social Forestry

Common categories include:

  • Farm forestry.
  • Community forestry.
  • Extension forestry.
  • Agroforestry.
85. Farm Forestry
  • Farmers grow trees on private agricultural land.
  • Trees may be planted:
  • On boundaries.
  • In unused patches.
  • Along irrigation channels.
86. Community Forestry
  • Trees are planted on community lands.
  • Benefits are intended for local people.
87. Extension Forestry
  • Trees are planted outside traditional forest areas.
  • Examples include:
  • Roadsides.
  • Canal banks.
  • Railway margins.
88. Agroforestry
  • Agroforestry combines trees with:
  • Crops.
  • Livestock.
  • It can diversify farm income and improve soil and microclimate.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Agroforestry → Trees + Crops/Livestock

89. Silviculture
  • Silviculture is the science and practice of establishing, tending and managing forest stands.
📌 Must-Memorise

Silviculture → Forest Cultivation and Management

90. Afforestation
  • Afforestation means establishing tree cover on land that was not recently forested or on degraded non-forest land.
91. Reforestation
  • Reforestation means restoring forest cover on previously forested land that has been cleared or degraded.
92. Deforestation
  • Deforestation is large-scale removal or conversion of forest cover.
  • It may result from:
  • Agriculture.
  • Mining.
  • Roads.
  • Dams.
  • Settlements.
  • Logging.
93. Effects of Deforestation

Deforestation can cause:

  • Soil erosion.
  • Biodiversity loss.
  • Reduced carbon storage.
  • Habitat fragmentation.
  • Changes in runoff.
  • Increased landslide risk on steep terrain.
94. Habitat Fragmentation
  • Fragmentation divides a continuous habitat into smaller isolated patches.
  • It can restrict wildlife movement and reduce genetic exchange.
95. Forest Degradation
  • Forest degradation means decline in forest quality without complete removal of the forest.
  • Causes include:
  • Repeated fires.
  • Overgrazing.
  • Excess fuelwood extraction.
  • Invasive species.
  • Unsustainable logging.
96. Forest Fire
  • Forest fire is an uncontrolled fire in forest or grassland vegetation.
  • Fires can be:
  • Natural.
  • Human-caused.
  • Dry deciduous and pine forests can be particularly fire-prone.
97. Causes of Forest Fires

Causes include:

  • Lightning.
  • Agricultural burning.
  • Campfires.
  • Cigarettes.
  • Deliberate burning.
  • Dry vegetation.
98. Effects of Forest Fires

Fires may cause:

  • Vegetation loss.
  • Wildlife mortality.
  • Soil damage.
  • Air pollution.
  • Carbon emissions.
  • Increased erosion.
99. Fire Ecology
  • Some ecosystems are adapted to occasional fire.
  • However, frequent or intense fires can cause long-term ecological degradation.
100. Forest Fire Prevention

Measures include:

  • Fire lines.
  • Early detection.
  • Controlled removal of dry fuel.
  • Public awareness.
  • Rapid response.
  • Satellite monitoring.
101. Fire Line
  • A fire line is a strip cleared of combustible vegetation.
  • It helps slow or stop the spread of fire.
102. Forest and Tribal Communities
  • Many tribal and forest-dependent communities rely on forests for:
  • Food.
  • Fodder.
  • Fuel.
  • Medicines.
  • Cultural practices.
  • Livelihoods.
103. Non-Timber Forest Products

NTFPs include forest products other than conventional timber.

Examples include:

  • Honey.
  • Bamboo.
  • Tendu leaves.
  • Gums.
  • Resins.
  • Medicinal plants.
  • Fruits.
  • Seeds.
📌 Must-Memorise

NTFP → Forest Product Other Than Timber

104. Minor Forest Produce
  • The term minor forest produce is traditionally used for several non-timber products.
  • These products are often economically important to forest communities.
105. Resin
  • Resin is obtained from certain trees.
  • It is used in:
  • Varnishes.
  • Adhesives.
  • Chemicals.
106. Gum
  • Natural gums are plant exudates.
  • They have pharmaceutical, food and industrial uses.
107. Lac
  • Lac is a resinous material secreted by lac insects living on host trees.
  • It is used to make shellac and related products.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Lac → Insect-Derived Forest Product

108. Medicinal Plants
  • Indian forests contain numerous medicinal plants.
  • Sustainable harvesting is necessary because over-collection can threaten wild populations.
109. Sandalwood
  • Sandalwood is valued for aromatic heartwood and oil.
  • Southern India is historically famous for sandalwood.
🔗 Tamil Nadu Key Link

Sandalwood → Southern India

110. Sandalwood in Tamil Nadu
  • Sandalwood occurs naturally in parts of Tamil Nadu's dry deciduous and scrub forest zones.
  • The Eastern Ghats and adjoining interior hills contain suitable habitats.
111. Red Sanders
  • Red sanders is a valuable tree native to parts of the southern Eastern Ghats.
  • It is especially associated with Andhra Pradesh.
  • It should not be confused with ordinary sandalwood.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Red Sanders ≠ Sandalwood

112. Forest-Based Industries

Forests provide raw materials for:

  • Paper.
  • Plywood.
  • Furniture.
  • Match industry.
  • Rayon-related cellulose industries.
  • Handicrafts.
113. Pulpwood
  • Pulpwood is wood used to make paper pulp.
  • Fast-growing plantation species are often used.
114. Forest Plantation
  • Plantations may consist of one or a few selected commercial species.
  • Plantation forest should not automatically be treated as ecologically equivalent to natural forest.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Plantation ≠ Natural Forest in Biodiversity Value

115. Monoculture Plantation
  • Monoculture means growing a single species over a large area.
  • It can simplify ecosystems and increase vulnerability to pests or disease.
116. Joint Forest Management
  • Joint Forest Management involves cooperation between forest departments and local communities in protection and management.
  • Communities may receive certain benefits from improved forests.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

JFM → Forest Department + Local Community

117. Forest Conservation

Important methods include:

  • Protected areas.
  • Afforestation.
  • Reforestation.
  • Social forestry.
  • Sustainable harvesting.
  • Fire management.
  • Community participation.
118. Watershed Forests
  • Forests in upper catchments influence downstream water supply.
  • Their conservation reduces:
  • Sedimentation.
  • Flash runoff.
  • Soil loss.
119. Forest and Reservoir Sedimentation
  • Deforestation in catchments increases erosion.
  • Sediment enters reservoirs.
  • Reservoir storage capacity declines.
120. Forests and Landslides
  • Root systems can improve slope stability.
  • Forest removal on steep slopes may increase landslide susceptibility, especially during heavy rainfall.
121. Western Ghats Forests

The Western Ghats contain:

  • Evergreen forests.
  • Semi-evergreen forests.
  • Moist deciduous forests.
  • Dry deciduous forests.
  • Shola-grassland systems.
📌 Must-Memorise

Western Ghats → Very High Forest Diversity

122. Western Ghats Rainfall Gradient
  • Western windward slopes receive heavy rainfall.
  • Forests become progressively drier toward interior rain-shadow regions.
123. Northeastern Forests

Northeastern India contains:

  • Tropical evergreen forests.
  • Semi-evergreen forests.
  • Moist deciduous forests.
  • Subtropical and montane forests at higher elevations.
124. Central Indian Forest Belt

Large forest regions occur in:

  • Madhya Pradesh.
  • Chhattisgarh.
  • Maharashtra.
  • Odisha.
  • Jharkhand.

These are dominated largely by deciduous forests.

125. Central India — Sal and Teak Pattern
  • Sal is important in more eastern and northeastern central Indian forests.
  • Teak is prominent in western and southern central Indian forests.
126. Himalayan Forests

Himalayan forests change from:

  • Tropical/subtropical foothill forests.
  • Temperate forests.
  • Conifers.
  • Subalpine forests.
  • Alpine vegetation.
127. Andaman and Nicobar Forests
  • High rainfall supports dense tropical evergreen and semi-evergreen forests.
  • Mangroves are also extensive along suitable coasts.
  • Island forests contain high levels of endemism.
128. Lakshadweep Vegetation
  • Lakshadweep has limited natural forest because islands are small and low-lying.
  • Coconut vegetation dominates much of the inhabited landscape.
129. Forests and Biodiversity Hotspots

Parts of India fall within globally recognised biodiversity hotspots.

Important forest-rich hotspot regions include:

  • Western Ghats.
  • Himalaya.
  • Indo-Burma region.
  • Sundaland component represented by Nicobar Islands.

Detailed biodiversity facts follow in the next chapter.

130. Endemism
  • An endemic species is naturally restricted to a particular geographical area.
  • Western Ghats and island forests contain many endemic species.
131. Forest Corridors
  • Wildlife corridors connect separated habitat patches.
  • They allow:
  • Animal movement.
  • Seasonal migration.
  • Genetic exchange.
132. Elephant Corridors
  • Elephant corridors connect forest habitats used by elephant populations.
  • Fragmentation can increase human-elephant conflict.
133. Human-Wildlife Conflict

Forest fragmentation and land-use change can increase:

  • Crop damage.
  • Livestock loss.
  • Encounters between people and wildlife.
134. Forest Conservation and Wildlife
  • Forest conservation protects habitat.
  • Wildlife conservation cannot be separated from landscape and forest management.
135. Tamil Nadu Forest Geography — Overview

Tamil Nadu's forests occur mainly in:

  • Western Ghats.
  • Eastern Ghats.
  • Nilgiris.
  • Anaimalai Hills.
  • Palani Hills.
  • Kalakkad-Mundanthurai region.
  • Dry interior hill ranges.
  • Coastal mangroves.
136. Tamil Nadu Major Forest Types

Important forest types include:

  • Tropical evergreen.
  • Semi-evergreen.
  • Moist deciduous.
  • Dry deciduous.
  • Thorn forests.
  • Montane shola.
  • Mangroves.
🔗 Tamil Nadu Key Link

Tamil Nadu → Very High Forest-Type Diversity

137. Nilgiri Forests

Nilgiris contain:

  • Shola forests.
  • Montane grasslands.
  • Evergreen forests at suitable elevations.
  • Moist deciduous forests at lower levels.
138. Anaimalai Forests
  • Anaimalai Hills contain:
  • Evergreen forests.
  • Semi-evergreen forests.
  • Moist deciduous forests.
  • Shola systems at higher elevations.
  • They are biologically rich.
139. Palani Hills
  • Palani Hills contain montane forests and grasslands.
  • Kodaikanal lies within this highland region.
140. Kalakkad-Mundanthurai Forests
  • Kalakkad-Mundanthurai lies in the southern Western Ghats.
  • The region contains evergreen and moist forest ecosystems.
  • It is an important wildlife and watershed landscape.
📌 Tamil Nadu Must-Memorise

Kalakkad-Mundanthurai → Southern Western Ghats Forests

141. Agasthyamalai / Pothigai Forests
  • Agasthyamalai forms part of the southern Western Ghats.
  • It contains very rich evergreen forests.
  • It is a major biodiversity and watershed region.
142. Eastern Ghats Forests of Tamil Nadu

Important hill systems include:

  • Javadi Hills.
  • Shevaroy Hills.
  • Kalrayan Hills.
  • Kolli Hills.
  • Pachamalai.
143. Eastern Ghats Forest Character
  • Eastern Ghats forests are generally drier than the wettest Western Ghats forests.
  • Dry deciduous and mixed forest formations are widespread.
  • Local moist forest occurs where rainfall and altitude permit.
144. Thorn Forests of Tamil Nadu
  • Thorn and scrub vegetation occurs in dry interior districts.
  • Common plants include:
  • Acacia-type species.
  • Euphorbia.
  • Dry scrub.
145. Tamil Nadu Shola Forests

Important shola landscapes occur in:

  • Nilgiris.
  • Palani Hills.
  • Anaimalai.
  • High southern Western Ghats.
146. Shola Threats

Shola-grassland ecosystems face pressures from:

  • Invasive species.
  • Plantation conversion.
  • Fire.
  • Roads.
  • Tourism.
  • Climate change.
147. Invasive Plant Species
  • Invasive species are non-native species that spread and cause ecological harm.
  • They can alter forest structure and suppress native vegetation.
148. Lantana camara
  • Lantana is a major invasive shrub in many Indian forests.
  • It can form dense thickets and reduce native vegetation.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Lantana → Invasive Forest Shrub

149. Prosopis juliflora
  • Prosopis juliflora is an introduced thorny species widespread in many dry regions.
  • It can spread aggressively and alter native dryland ecosystems.
150. Wattle in Nilgiris
  • Acacia/wattle plantations and invasions have altered parts of the Nilgiri shola-grassland landscape.
  • Restoration efforts often focus on native shola and grassland recovery.
151. Eucalyptus
  • Eucalyptus species have been widely planted for:
  • Pulpwood.
  • Timber.
  • Fuelwood.
  • Large monoculture plantations may alter local ecosystem conditions.
152. Pichavaram Forest Resource Importance

Pichavaram mangroves provide:

  • Coastal protection.
  • Fish nursery habitat.
  • Carbon storage.
  • Bird habitat.
  • Local livelihoods.
153. Muthupet Forest Resource Importance

Muthupet mangroves help:

  • Protect the Kaveri delta coast.
  • Support fisheries.
  • Provide bird habitat.
  • Stabilise coastal sediments.
154. Forests and Tamil Nadu Rivers

Western Ghats forests form catchments for rivers including:

  • Kaveri tributaries.
  • Bhavani.
  • Tamiraparani.
  • Vaigai tributary systems.
  • Numerous shorter streams.
155. Forests and Tamil Nadu Water Security
  • Hill forests regulate runoff.
  • They protect reservoirs from excessive siltation.
  • They contribute to stream flow and groundwater recharge.
156. Sandalwood and Eastern Ghats
  • Parts of the Eastern Ghats and interior Tamil Nadu historically support sandalwood.
  • Sandalwood is highly valuable and requires protection from illegal cutting.
157. Forest-Based Livelihoods in Tamil Nadu

Forest communities may depend on:

  • Honey.
  • Medicinal plants.
  • Tamarind.
  • Fodder.
  • Bamboo.
  • Other non-timber products.
158. Forest Conservation Challenges in Tamil Nadu

Major challenges include:

  • Fragmentation.
  • Forest fire.
  • Invasive plants.
  • Encroachment.
  • Quarrying.
  • Roads.
  • Tourism pressure.
  • Human-wildlife conflict.
159. Forest Fire in Western and Eastern Ghats
  • Dry-season fires can damage both Western and Eastern Ghats forests.
  • Dry deciduous forests are especially susceptible during prolonged dry conditions.
160. Forest and Tourism

Unregulated tourism can lead to:

  • Waste.
  • Road expansion.
  • Wildlife disturbance.
  • Increased fire risk.
  • Habitat fragmentation.
161. Forest Restoration

Forest restoration may include:

  • Natural regeneration.
  • Native-species planting.
  • Invasive-species removal.
  • Soil and water conservation.
  • Fire management.
162. Natural Regeneration
  • Natural regeneration allows forests to recover through existing seeds, roots and nearby vegetation.
  • It can preserve local genetic diversity better than unsuitable monoculture planting.
163. Assisted Natural Regeneration
  • Assisted natural regeneration protects naturally emerging seedlings and removes pressures such as grazing or repeated fire.
164. Native Species
  • Native species occur naturally in a geographical region.
  • Using appropriate native species generally supports local biodiversity better than exotic monocultures.
165. Exotic Species
  • Exotic species are introduced from outside their natural range.
  • Some remain harmless, while others become invasive.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Exotic Species ≠ Automatically Invasive

166. Sustainable Forest Management

Sustainable management aims to maintain:

  • Forest productivity.
  • Biodiversity.
  • Soil.
  • Water.
  • Carbon storage.
  • Community benefits.
167. Selective Felling
  • Selective felling removes chosen trees rather than clearing an entire forest.
  • Poorly managed selective logging can still cause ecological damage.
168. Clear Felling
  • Clear felling removes most or all trees from a particular area.
  • It creates much greater immediate habitat disturbance.
169. Forest Certification — Concept
  • Forest certification systems aim to identify forest products sourced from responsibly managed forests.
  • They encourage sustainable harvesting and supply-chain transparency.
170. Forest Resource Conservation Hierarchy

A sound approach includes:

  • Protect natural forests.
  • Restore degraded forests.
  • Reduce waste.
  • Recycle wood and paper.
  • Use plantations responsibly.
  • Support community management.
171. Paper Recycling
  • Recycling paper reduces demand for virgin pulp.
  • It also saves energy and water in many production systems.
172. Forests and Sustainable Development

Forests contribute to:

  • Water security.
  • Food security.
  • Livelihoods.
  • Disaster-risk reduction.
  • Climate regulation.
  • Biodiversity conservation.
173. TNPSC High-Yield Pairings
  • Evergreen → High rainfall.
  • Deciduous → Monsoon forest.
  • Teak → Deciduous.
  • Sal → Northern/eastern deciduous.
  • Bamboo → Grass.
  • Tendu → Bidi.
  • Thorn forest → Rajasthan/dry regions.
  • Xerophyte → Dry adaptation.
  • Deodar → Western Himalaya.
  • Shola → Southern Western Ghats.
  • Mangrove → Tidal coast.
  • Pneumatophore → Breathing root.
  • Sundarbans → Mangrove.
  • Pichavaram → Tamil Nadu mangrove.
  • Muthupet → Tamil Nadu mangrove.
  • Social forestry → Community needs.
  • Agroforestry → Trees + crops.
  • Silviculture → Forest management.
  • JFM → Community + Forest Department.
  • NTFP → Non-timber forest product.
  • Lantana → Invasive shrub.
  • Nilgiris → Shola-grassland.
  • Kalakkad-Mundanthurai → Southern Western Ghats.
174. TNPSC Traps
  • Forest is not only a source of timber.
  • Forests are renewable only if sustainably managed.
  • Tropical deciduous forests are India's most widespread forest type.
  • Evergreen trees do not shed all leaves simultaneously.
  • Teak and sal are not typical mangrove species.
  • Bamboo is botanically a grass.
  • Thorn forests are adapted to low rainfall.
  • Xerophytes are drought-adapted plants.
  • Deodar is a Himalayan conifer.
  • Shola forests occur in southern Western Ghats highlands.
  • Mangroves grow in tidal saline environments.
  • Pneumatophores are aerial breathing roots.
  • Sundarbans lie in the Ganga-Brahmaputra delta.
  • Pichavaram and Muthupet are in Tamil Nadu.
  • Reserved forest and protected forest are not identical categories.
  • Recorded forest area and actual forest cover are not identical.
  • Social forestry mainly aims to meet community needs and reduce pressure on natural forests.
  • Agroforestry combines trees with agriculture or livestock.
  • Silviculture means forest cultivation and management.
  • Afforestation and reforestation are not exactly the same.
  • NTFPs can be economically important even though they are not timber.
  • Plantation forest is not ecologically identical to natural forest.
  • Exotic species are not automatically invasive.
  • Forest fire is not always entirely natural.
  • Forest conservation is closely connected with water and soil conservation.
175. Ultra-Short Memory Chain
  • Forest → Renewable if managed.
  • Evergreen → High rainfall.
  • Deciduous → Most widespread.
  • Teak → Timber.
  • Sal → East/north.
  • Bamboo → Grass.
  • Tendu → Bidi.
  • Thorn → Dry.
  • Xerophyte → Drought.
  • Deodar → Himalaya.
  • Shola → South Western Ghats.
  • Mangrove → Tidal.
  • Pneumatophore → Breathing root.
  • Sundarbans → Bengal delta.
  • Pichavaram → TN.
  • Muthupet → TN.
  • Social forestry → Community.
  • Agroforestry → Trees + crops.
  • Silviculture → Forest management.
  • JFM → Community partnership.
  • Lantana → Invasive.
  • Nilgiris → Shola.
  • Kalakkad-Mundanthurai → Southern Ghats.
Rapid Revision — TNPSC Most Expected
  • What are forest resources? → Biological and ecological resources obtained from forest ecosystems.
  • Are forests renewable? → Yes, only when regeneration keeps pace with use.
  • Major ecological roles of forests? → Soil conservation, water regulation, carbon storage and biodiversity protection.
  • What is a carbon sink? → A system that absorbs more carbon than it releases.
  • Main factors controlling Indian forest distribution? → Rainfall, temperature, altitude, soil and relief.
  • Major Indian forest types? → Evergreen, deciduous, thorn, montane and mangrove forests.
  • Where are tropical evergreen forests found? → Western Ghats, northeastern India and Andaman-Nicobar Islands.
  • Main feature of evergreen forests? → Trees do not shed all leaves at the same time.
  • Important evergreen hardwoods? → Ebony and rosewood.
  • Most widespread natural forest type in India? → Tropical deciduous forest.
  • Other name for tropical deciduous forest? → Monsoon forest.
  • Two divisions of deciduous forest? → Moist and dry deciduous.
  • Important timber tree of central and peninsular deciduous forests? → Teak.
  • Important tree of northern/eastern moist deciduous forests? → Sal.
  • Tendu leaves are used for? → Bidi making.
  • Bamboo is botanically what? → Grass.
  • Where are tropical thorn forests found? → Rajasthan, Gujarat and other dry regions.
  • What is a xerophyte? → Plant adapted to dry conditions.
  • Important desert tree of Rajasthan? → Khejri.
  • What happens to vegetation with altitude in Himalayas? → It changes from subtropical to temperate, subalpine and alpine types.
  • Important western Himalayan conifer? → Deodar.
  • What are shola forests? → Montane evergreen forest patches of the southern Western Ghats.
  • Where are shola forests important in Tamil Nadu? → Nilgiris, Anaimalai and Palani Hills.
  • What are mangroves? → Salt-tolerant tidal coastal forests.
  • Where do mangroves grow? → Deltas, estuaries, tidal creeks and mudflats.
  • What are pneumatophores? → Aerial breathing roots of waterlogged plants such as mangroves.
  • What are prop roots? → Supporting roots extending into soft tidal soil.
  • What is vivipary? → Seed germination while still attached to the parent plant.
  • Largest famous mangrove delta region? → Sundarbans.
  • Sundarbans are associated with which delta? → Ganga-Brahmaputra-Meghna delta.
  • Important Tamil Nadu mangroves? → Pichavaram and Muthupet.
  • Pichavaram is associated with? → Vellar-Coleroon estuarine region.
  • Muthupet is associated with? → Kaveri delta coast.
  • What is blue carbon? → Carbon stored in coastal ecosystems such as mangroves and seagrass.
  • Traditional legal forest categories? → Reserved, protected and unclassed forests.
  • Which traditional category has the highest legal protection? → Reserved forests.
  • Is recorded forest area the same as forest cover? → No.
  • What is social forestry? → Tree planting to meet community needs and reduce pressure on natural forests.
  • What is farm forestry? → Trees grown on private farm land.
  • What is agroforestry? → Combination of trees with crops or livestock.
  • What is silviculture? → Science and practice of managing forest stands.
  • What is afforestation? → Establishing tree cover on non-forest/degraded land.
  • What is reforestation? → Restoring trees on previously forested land.
  • What is forest degradation? → Loss of forest quality without complete forest removal.
  • What is habitat fragmentation? → Breaking a continuous habitat into isolated patches.
  • What is a fire line? → Vegetation-free strip used to slow forest fires.
  • What is NTFP? → Non-Timber Forest Product.
  • Examples of NTFPs? → Honey, bamboo, gums, resins, medicinal plants and tendu leaves.
  • What is lac? → Resinous material produced by lac insects.
  • What is Joint Forest Management? → Cooperative forest management involving local communities and forest authorities.
  • Important invasive shrub in Indian forests? → Lantana camara.
  • Important introduced thorny invasive plant of many dry regions? → Prosopis juliflora.
  • Which Tamil Nadu mountain region is famous for shola-grassland ecosystems? → Nilgiris.
  • Important southern Tamil Nadu Western Ghats forest landscape? → Kalakkad-Mundanthurai.
  • Which hills form a major evergreen forest region of southern Tamil Nadu? → Agasthyamalai/Pothigai Hills.
  • Main forest types found in Tamil Nadu? → Evergreen, semi-evergreen, deciduous, thorn, shola and mangrove forests.
  • Why are Western Ghats forests important for Tamil Nadu water resources? → They protect river catchments and regulate runoff.
  • How does deforestation affect reservoirs? → Increased erosion causes greater sedimentation.
  • Why are forests important on steep slopes? → They reduce erosion and help stabilise soil.
  • Is plantation forest ecologically equivalent to natural forest? → No.
  • What is natural regeneration? → Forest recovery from existing seeds, roots and nearby vegetation.
  • What is sustainable forest management? → Forest use that maintains productivity, biodiversity and ecological functions over time.
